1.title: Kubernetes Architecture, API and Objects
1.text: Welcome to Module 2: Kubernetes Architecture, API and Objects. This module is in the Kubernetes Fundamentals domain, and it covers the first part of the topic called Kubernetes Core Concepts. By the end you will be able to do five things. Name the control plane and node components, and what each does. Explain declarative configuration and reconciliation. Read the A P I's groups, versions and kinds, and the parts of a manifest. Use labels, selectors, annotations, namespaces and owner references. And recognize custom resources, operators and the ways to get a cluster.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Gets a Cluster
1.text: At Harbor Books, the platform engineer is handed a new cluster and has to learn what is inside it. The team will describe the shop in files and let Kubernetes make it so. People will need to find all the storefront Pods, and to keep staging apart from production. In this module you map the parts of the cluster, and the objects the team will use.

1.title: A Cluster: Control Plane and Nodes
1.text: A cluster is a control plane plus worker nodes. The control plane makes global decisions, and it manages the nodes and the Pods. Nodes are the worker machines that run the Pods, and a node can be a virtual machine or a physical machine. In production, the control plane usually runs across several machines. The diagram shows the five control plane components above three nodes, each running a kube let, a kube proxy and some Pods. Exam tip: the control plane decides, and the nodes run the Pods.

1.title: Control Plane Components
1.text: The control plane has up to five components. The kube A P I server serves the Kubernetes A P I, and it is the front end of the control plane. E T C D keeps all cluster data in a consistent, highly available key value store. The kube scheduler picks a node for each new Pod that has none. The kube controller manager runs the controllers that keep the cluster at its desired state. And the cloud controller manager links the cluster to a cloud provider's A P I. A local or on-premises cluster has none. Because E T C D holds all cluster data, it needs a backup plan. Exam tip: the A P I server is the front door, E T C D is the memory, the scheduler places Pods and the controller manager runs the loops.

1.title: Node Components and Add-ons
1.text: Every node runs a few components. The kube let is an agent that makes sure the containers of its Pods are running. Kube proxy is a network proxy that implements part of the Service idea. It is optional, because some network plugins do the job themselves. The container runtime runs the containers, as you saw in module one. Add-ons extend the cluster, and every cluster should have cluster D N S. Exam tip: kube let and kube proxy run on every node. The scheduler and the A P I server do not.

1.title: Following a Request: From kubectl to a Running Pod
1.text: Follow one request through the cluster. You send it with kube control to the A P I server. The object is stored in E T C D. The scheduler notices a Pod with no node, and picks a node. The kube let on that node starts the containers and reports status. The components talk to each other through the A P I server, and never directly. Exam tip: when a question asks who stores, who places and who runs, the answers are E T C D, the scheduler and the kube let.

1.title: Declarative Versus Imperative
1.text: There are three ways to manage objects. Imperative commands work on live objects, for example kube control create deployment with an image. Imperative object configuration works on individual files, with kube control create dash f. And declarative object configuration works on directories of files, with kube control apply dash f. Declarative means you state the desired result in files, and Kubernetes works out the steps. Kube control apply is the recommended way to manage applications in production. Exam tip: declarative describes the end state, and imperative gives the steps.

1.title: Controllers and the Reconciliation Loop
1.text: A controller is a control loop that watches the cluster's state through the A P I server. It acts to narrow the gap between the current state and the desired state. A thermostat is the classic example: it compares the room to the setting, and acts. The diagram shows the cycle: observe, compare, act, and repeat. The kube controller manager runs many controllers in one process. Exam tip: self-healing in Kubernetes is just controllers reconciling.

1.title: The API: Groups, Versions and Kinds
1.text: The A P I is organized into groups. The core group lives under slash A P I slash v one, and its A P I version is written as plain v one. It holds Pod, Service, Config Map and Namespace. Named groups live under slash A P I S, then the group, then the version. For example, apps slash v one holds Deployment and Stateful Set. And batch slash v one holds Job and Cron Job. Versions have levels. Alpha versions, like v one alpha one, are off by default, and support can be dropped at any time. Built-in beta versions are also off by default. Stable versions are named v X, with an integer. Exam tip: A P I version is group and version, and the core group is written as plain v one.

1.title: Anatomy of a Manifest
1.text: A manifest has a few required fields. A P I version says which version of the A P I you use. Kind says what kind of object it is. Metadata holds identifying data, such as a name, a U I D, which is a unique I D, and an optional namespace. And spec is the desired state, which you write. There is also status, the current state, which Kubernetes writes and keeps updated. The snippet is a minimal Pod. An object is a record of intent: after you create it, Kubernetes works to keep it that way. Exam tip: you write the spec, and Kubernetes writes the status.

1.title: Kinds You Will Meet
1.text: This slide is a map of kinds you will meet. A Pod is one or more containers run together. Deployment, Stateful Set, Daemon Set, Job and Cron Job are controllers that run Pods, in module three. Config Map and Secret hold configuration and sensitive settings, in module four. Service and Ingress give stable network access to Pods, in module six. A Persistent Volume Claim is a request for storage, in module seven. And Namespace and Node are covered in this module. Exam tip: learn the kind names now, and the next modules explain each one.

1.title: kubectl: the Command Line
1.text: Kube control talks to the cluster's control plane through the A P I. You use it to create, inspect, update and delete objects. The syntax is kube control, then a command, a type, a name, and flags. Resource types are case insensitive, and names are case sensitive. Kube control explain documents a resource, and kube control A P I resources lists the kinds. The snippet shows get, describe, apply and delete. Exam tip: get lists, describe explains, apply declares, and delete removes.

1.title: kubeconfig: Clusters, Users and Contexts
1.text: A kube config file lists clusters, users and contexts. A context ties a cluster, a user and a namespace together, and current context says which one is active. By default, kube control reads the config file in the dot kube folder of your home directory. The kube config environment variable, or the kube config flag, points elsewhere. Kube control config get contexts lists contexts, and kube control config use context switches. Use kube config files only from trusted sources. Exam tip: the context decides which cluster, user and namespace the next command uses.

1.title: Labels, Selectors and Annotations
1.text: Labels are key value pairs on objects. They hold identifying attributes that are meaningful to users. A selector filters objects by their labels, and selecting by label is the main way Kubernetes groups objects. Services and controllers use selectors to find their Pods. In the diagram, the selector app equals storefront picks the first two Pods. Annotations are different. They hold non-identifying metadata for tools and people, and they can be large and unstructured. Exam tip: labels select, and annotations do not.

1.title: Namespaces and Owner References
1.text: Namespaces isolate groups of resources within one cluster. A name must be unique inside one namespace, and another namespace may reuse it. Namespaces cannot be nested, and each object is in one namespace. Four start with every cluster: default, kube node lease, kube public and kube system. Owner references record which objects depend on which, so the control plane cleans up the right ones. For example, a Replica Set owns its Pods. Ownership is not the same as labels and selectors. Exam tip: a namespace scopes names and policies, and ownership drives clean-up.

1.title: Custom Resources, Controllers and Operators
1.text: You can extend the A P I. A Custom Resource Definition, or C R D, adds a new kind to the A P I, without building a custom A P I server. Custom resources are the objects of that kind, and you use them with kube control just like built-in objects. A custom controller keeps them at their desired state. The operator pattern links a controller to custom resources, to automate what a human operator would do. Exam tip: a C R D adds a kind, and an operator adds the controller that acts on it.

2.title: Where Clusters Come From
2.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. You can choose a managed service, instead of running the cluster yourself. Self-managed means you run the control plane and the nodes yourself. Kube A D M is a tool that installs Kubernetes and sets up a secure cluster. Kind runs local clusters that use Docker containers as nodes. Mini kube is a local cluster for Mac, Linux and Windows. And K three S is lightweight, fully conformant Kubernetes in a single binary. Exam tip: kube A D M builds clusters, kind and mini kube are for learning, and K three S is the lightweight one.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Architecture
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Control plane or node: the A P I server, E T C D, scheduler and controller manager decide, while the kube let and kube proxy run on every node. Declarative or imperative: declarative states the result and uses apply. Spec or status: you write the spec, and Kubernetes writes the status. Label or annotation: labels select, and annotations only inform. Group or version: apps slash v one is group and version, and the core group is plain v one. C R D or operator: a C R D adds a kind, and an operator adds a controller for it. Exam tip: picture the request path.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. A cluster has a control plane, with the A P I server, E T C D, scheduler and controller manager, and nodes, with the kube let, kube proxy and runtime. Declarative means you state the desired result, and controllers reconcile the current state toward it. The A P I has groups and versions, and a manifest has kind, metadata, spec and status. You use kube control and a kube config. Labels select, annotations inform, namespaces scope names, and owner references drive clean-up. And C R Ds add kinds, while operators add controllers. Now eleven practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Where does Kubernetes keep all of its cluster data? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. E T C D is the backing store for all cluster data, which is why it needs a backup plan. The kube let runs Pods, the scheduler picks nodes, and the runtime's image cache holds images, not cluster state.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A Harbor Books Pod has been created but is not yet assigned to any node. Which component picks a node for it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The kube scheduler watches for new Pods with no node and selects one. The kube let runs the Pods that are assigned to its node, kube proxy maintains network rules, and E T C D only stores data.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. What does the kube let do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The kube let is the agent on each node that makes sure the containers of its Pods are running. Choosing nodes is the scheduler's job, the controller loops belong to the controller manager, and network rules belong to kube proxy.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. The Harbor Books team keeps its storefront manifests in a directory and wants Kubernetes to create or update whatever differs. Which command follows the declarative approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Declarative configuration states the desired result in files, and kube control apply makes the cluster match them. Creating a Deployment from flags and scaling it are imperative commands, and deleting removes objects.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A controller finds fewer running Pods than the desired state asks for. What does it do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A controller is a control loop. It compares the current state with the desired state and acts to close the gap. It does not wait for approval, it does not edit the spec you wrote, and it keeps watching.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which A P I version belongs in a Deployment manifest? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Deployments are in the apps group, version v one, written apps slash v one. The core group is written as plain v one and holds kinds such as Pod and Service. Batch slash v one holds Jobs and Cron Jobs, and an alpha version is off by default.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which statement about A P I versions is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Stable versions are named v X, where X is an integer. Alpha versions are off by default and may be dropped at any time. Built-in beta versions are also off by default. And no version name contains the word stable.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A Service must find all the storefront Pods. Which feature does it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Selecting by label is how Services and controllers find their Pods: they pick the Pods whose labels match. Annotations are not used to select, owner references drive clean-up, and a namespace scopes names rather than choosing Pods.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Two teams want to use the same object name in one cluster without a clash. What provides the separation? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A name must be unique inside one namespace, and another namespace may reuse it, so two teams can each use their own. Labels and annotations do not scope names, and the U I D is generated by Kubernetes in addition to the name.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. What does a Custom Resource Definition do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A C R D defines a new kind that is served by the existing A P I server, and its objects are used with kube control like built-in ones. Restarting containers is the kube let's job, node choice is scheduling, and backups are a separate task.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. The Harbor Books team installs software that adds a Database kind to the A P I, plus a controller that creates, backs up and repairs databases from those objects. What is this pattern called? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. An operator is a controller linked to custom resources that automates what a human operator would do. Kube proxy handles networking, a Replica Set keeps a number of Pods running, and the cloud controller manager talks to a cloud provider.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, C: E T C D holds all cluster data. Question two, A: the scheduler picks a node for a new Pod. Question three, D: the kube let makes sure its Pods' containers run. Question four, B: kube control apply is declarative. Question five, A: a controller closes the gap to the desired state. Question six, C: Deployments are in apps slash v one. Question seven, D: stable versions are v X with an integer. Question eight, B: a label selector picks the Pods. Question nine, C: names are unique within a namespace. Question ten, A: a C R D adds a kind. Question eleven, D: an operator is a controller plus custom resources.
